archetype.name: Game Manager (spot-starter backup)
archetype.definition: A ninth-year undrafted veteran asked to keep the offense on schedule with short, quick throws, who has historically survived on avoiding sacks rather than creating plays, and who is now Atlanta's third quarterback.

report.headline: Two ugly outings bought him a seat at QB3, and the tape explains why
report.take:
Cooper Rush has been the same quarterback for most of his career: a short-area distributor who wins games by not losing them. His 2024 season in Dallas is the template, with 10 games, 12 touchdowns, a 4-4 record and EPA per play of -0.079. That is replacement level but functional. This year he opened as Atlanta's Week 1 starter, gave way to Tua Tagovailoa in Week 2 (Rush still took 58% of the snaps), and has watched Michael Penix Jr. start every game since. The depth chart now lists him third. Whatever the numbers say, the most important fact on this card is that he isn't expected to play.

The numbers themselves are about as bad as a qualifier can post. He ranks 44th of 45 in EPA per dropback (-0.635) and dead last in interception rate (10.3%). His pace17 line projects 34 interceptions, which is not a real forecast, just a sign of how small and how ugly the sample is. The damage is concentrated, though. On throws under 10 air yards he was mediocre but not disastrous: the 0-9 band sat at -0.011 EPA with a 50% success rate. The wreckage came on just seven intermediate attempts, which produced three interceptions and -12.2 EPA, and on third downs, where he converted 15.4% while facing an average of 8.5 yards to go. When the offense asked him to push the ball past the sticks, it broke.

What the numbers hide is how out of character two pieces of this are. His CPOE fell 11.7 points from last year, and his bad-throw rate rose to 23.1%. Neither has ever been his profile: his accuracy has always been below expected, but not like this. More striking, he has always been one of the league's best at avoiding sacks once pressured. He ranked 2nd in pressure-to-sack rate in 2025 and 4th in 2022. This year 62.5% of his pressures became sacks behind a line that ranks 5th in hit rate allowed. Over 46 dropbacks, that looks like a rusty backup with no timing with this group of receivers, not a new identity. Even his top target tells the story. Drake London was productive on his nine targets, while Kyle Pitts and Bijan Robinson combined for heavy negative EPA on the rest.

Going forward, Rush is an emergency option and nothing more. If two quarterbacks ahead of him went down, the right expectation would be the 2024 version: dink-and-dunk, a run-heavy plan built on an offense ranked 3rd in rush EPA, and an interception rate that falls hard from 10% toward his career norm. That still makes him a low-ceiling passer, which is exactly why he is third on the depth chart.

strengths.title: Short game held near neutral
strengths.body: On throws under 10 air yards he was roughly break-even, with a 50% success rate in the 0-9 band. Throws to the left side were outright positive. That is the part of his game that has carried him through every spot start. It is sustainable because it reflects his low-aggressiveness, quick-release style rather than luck.

strengths.title: Track record as a functional fill-in
strengths.body: Before 2025 he was a usable short-term starter. In 2022 he won four of five games, and in 2024 he went .500 across ten games with 12 touchdowns. Those seasons were built on avoiding negative plays, which is why this year's turnover spike reads as an outlier rather than a new baseline.

strengths.title: London connection worked
strengths.body: Drake London was the one target who produced positive value with Rush, at +0.447 EPA per target on nine looks. If Rush is ever pressed into action, leaning on London rather than force-feeding the backs would be his cleanest path to competence.

concerns.title: Intermediate throws became turnovers
concerns.body: Three of his four interceptions came on just seven attempts at 10-19 air yards, and that band's EPA was catastrophic. This is the real limit on his game: he has never been a confident middle-of-the-field thrower, and without timing he became a liability there. The rate will regress on more volume, but the weakness is real.

concerns.title: Accuracy fell off a cliff
concerns.body: His CPOE dropped sharply from last season, and nearly a quarter of his throws were charted as bad. He has always been below expected, but not to this degree. That points to rust and unfamiliarity more than decline, though at nearly 33 it is not something to wave away entirely.

concerns.title: Sacks out of character
concerns.body: His pressure-to-sack rate this season contradicts his best career trait: he ranked 2nd in that stat in 2025. It happened behind a line that limits hits well. Combined with his failures on third down, it suggests he was holding the ball without answers rather than being overrun. Expect the rate to regress if he plays again.

trend.note: Week 2 was worse than Week 1 on fewer snaps: lower CPOE, more bad throws and a lost fumble. Atlanta has since started someone else for four straight weeks and slid him to third on the depth chart.

nextGame.headline: QB3 against the 49ers: no expected role, rough script if forced
nextGame.body:
Rush isn't projected to take a snap; Penix has started Weeks 3 through 6 and Rush sits at QB3. If he did play, San Francisco's defense ranks 5th in EPA and 2nd against the run. That would take away the run-first crutch Atlanta (3rd in rush EPA) uses to protect a weak passer. The 49ers are softer on short throws, which is his zone, but their offense ranks 1st in pass EPA. A trailing script would force him into the intermediate throws where his season fell apart.

Availability on the San Francisco side helps any Atlanta passer. Nick Bosa and starting safety Marques Sigle are both listed out. Atlanta's own injury report is empty, so there is no clear path to Rush seeing the field barring an in-game injury. He practiced fully and is active.

keyMatchups.title: Run game meets elite run defense
keyMatchups.body: Atlanta's offense is built on the ground, but San Francisco is among the league's stingiest run defenses and allows the fewest explosive runs. That pushes whichever quarterback plays into more true passing downs than this offense wants.

keyMatchups.title: Soft short-area pass defense
keyMatchups.body: The 49ers rank 21st in EPA allowed on short throws, the exact area where Rush is least damaging. That is the one door open to a low-aggressiveness passer.

keyMatchups.title: Bosa out lightens the rush
keyMatchups.body: With Bosa inactive, San Francisco's pass rush loses its top edge. That matters for any Atlanta quarterback who holds the ball, as Rush did this year.

nextGame.watch: Whether Penix and the QB2 come through healthy; nothing else puts Rush on the field.

restOfSeason.body:
The realistic forecast is zero. Rush is QB3 behind a starter who has held the job for four weeks, so his weekly output is a rounding error unless injuries pile up. If he were forced into a start, expect the 2024 version rather than this season's: short throws, a heavy run share, protection that limits hits, and an interception rate far below the current 10.3%. That still adds up to a below-average passer, roughly 150-210 yards with about one turnover a start, because the intermediate game and accuracy problems are longstanding weaknesses, magnified here, not inventions of a small sample.

What will regress is the extreme stuff: the pressure-to-sack rate, the interception rate and the CPOE collapse are all well outside his career range on 46 dropbacks. What will not change is his ceiling. He does not push the ball downfield (intended air yards of 5.34) and has never posted a high-end efficiency season with real volume.
